"use client"

import { useFormStatus } from "react-dom"
import { toast } from "sonner"

import { Button } from "@/components/ui/button"
import {
  Field,
  FieldGroup,
  FieldLabel,
  FieldSet,
} from "@/components/ui/field"
import { Input } from "@/components/ui/input"
import { Spinner } from "@/components/ui/spinner"
import { Textarea } from "@/components/ui/textarea"

import { contactFormAction } from "../lib/actions"

function SubmitButton() {
  const { pending } = useFormStatus()

  return (
    <Button type="submit" disabled={pending}>
      {pending ? (
        <>
          <Spinner data-icon="inline-start" />
          Sending...
        </>
      ) : (
        "Send message"
      )}
    </Button>
  )
}

function ContactFields() {
  const { pending } = useFormStatus()

  return (
    <FieldSet disabled={pending}>
      <FieldGroup>
        {/* Honeypot: real users never see or fill this field (hidden +
            off-screen). Bots that auto-fill every field will trip it. */}
        <input
          type="text"
          name="company"
          tabIndex={-1}
          autoComplete="off"
          aria-hidden="true"
          className="absolute left-[-9999px] h-px w-px opacity-0"
        />
        <Field>
          <FieldLabel htmlFor="name">Name</FieldLabel>
          <Input
            id="name"
            name="name"
            placeholder="Your name"
            required
            autoComplete="name"
          />
        </Field>
        <Field>
          <FieldLabel htmlFor="email">Email</FieldLabel>
          <Input
            id="email"
            name="email"
            type="email"
            placeholder="your.email@example.com"
            required
            autoComplete="email"
          />
        </Field>
        <Field>
          <FieldLabel htmlFor="message">Message</FieldLabel>
          <Textarea
            id="message"
            name="message"
            rows={5}
            placeholder="Speaking, a question about a book, or whatever you wanted to say."
            required
          />
        </Field>
        <Field orientation="horizontal">
          <SubmitButton />
        </Field>
      </FieldGroup>
    </FieldSet>
  )
}

export function ContactForm() {
  async function handleSubmit(formData: FormData) {
    const result = await contactFormAction(formData)

    if (result?.error) {
      toast.error(result.error)
      return
    }

    if (result?.success) {
      toast.success("Message sent successfully!")
    }
  }

  return (
    <form action={handleSubmit}>
      <ContactFields />
    </form>
  )
}

--- title: RIP Pluto description: My take on the 2006 redefinition, the Kuiper Belt, and why my childhood poster of nine planets still stings a little. date: 2026-05-18 published: true --- People still ask me, half joking, whether Pluto is a planet. I understand the loyalty. I grew up with nine names in a row, taped to a bedroom wall, and childhood lists feel like contracts. When the International Astronomical Union changed the rules in 2006, a lot of people heard a demotion handed down by humorless bureaucrats. It was astronomy catching up with a crowded neighborhood — and I still flinch at the empty ninth slot. The IAU settled on three tests for a planet in our solar system. It must orbit the Sun. It must be round enough that gravity has pulled it into hydrostatic equilibrium — roughly spherical. And it must have cleared the neighborhood around its orbit. Pluto passes the first two. It fails the third. Clearing the neighborhood does not mean an empty sky. It means a body is gravitationally dominant along its path: it has swept up, ejected, or otherwise controlled the debris that shares its orbital zone. Earth has done this. Jupiter has done this with authority. Pluto has not. It travels through the Kuiper Belt, a broad ring of icy leftovers beyond Neptune, among peers of similar scale. That is the heart of it. Once we found Eris, and kept finding other large Kuiper Belt objects, the old nine-planet list stopped describing the solar system we actually live in. Keep Pluto as a planet under the old habits, and you soon have a dozen or more — not a tidy classroom poster, but an honest census of small worlds at the edge. > Pluto did not get smaller. Our map got larger. New Horizons showed mountains of water ice, a heart-shaped plain, a thin blue haze. Dwarf planet is the category that matches where it lives: among the cold, crowded outskirts, not among the eight bodies that own their lanes. I still miss the poster. I just stopped arguing with the belt.

--- title: How big is far description: How I talk about light-minutes, light-hours, and why the solar system is mostly empty room with a few bright furniture pieces. date: 2026-03-12 published: true --- Ask someone how far Mars is and you will usually get a number that sounds large and means almost nothing. Millions of kilometers are hard to feel. When I talk about distance in public, I count *time for light* instead of kilometers. Light leaves the Sun and reaches Earth in a little over eight minutes. That is already a useful unit: one astronomical unit is eight light-minutes of emptiness with a warm rock at one end. Saturn is more than an hour away at light speed when the geometry is cooperative — longer when it is not. Voyager 1, still outbound, is measured in light-*days*. The nearest other star is measured in years. The galaxy is a structure you cannot cross in a human lifetime at any speed we know how to build. I want the solar system to feel correctly sparse. Planets are lonely objects separated by volumes of almost nothing, held in place by gravity that does not care how empty the gaps look from here. > Far is a clock. Once you have that clock, conjunctions and spacecraft delay make more sense. The night sky is a set of delayed messages from objects that are still out there, doing physics, whether or not anyone is watching.

--- title: What the sky is made of description: My note on vacuum, photons, and why empty space is still full of rules. date: 2026-02-04 published: true --- On a clear night the sky looks like a black sheet with lights stuck to it. That is a useful lie, and I still catch myself believing it for a second. The black is a long look through vacuum — and vacuum is not empty the way a drawer is empty. It is a place where light can travel for years without hitting much of anything. What you see is almost entirely photons. Some left a nearby star minutes or years ago. Some bounced off the Moon. A few are the washed-out glow of our own atmosphere scattering sunlight long after sunset. The points are sources. The darkness between them is the path. There is more in that darkness than eyes report: magnetic fields, sparse gas, dust, neutrinos streaming through everything including you. None of that paints the sky blue at noon or black at midnight. The color of night is too little scattered light to overwhelm the retina. The physics is still there. I keep wonder attached to mechanism. The sky is radiation and geometry. Constellations are mnemonic overlays. And “empty” is a volume so thin that a photon can travel for years and still arrive.

--- title: The book that started it description: How one popular-science book turned my habit of looking up into a decision to study physics. date: 2025-11-22 published: true --- I became a physicist because a book made the night sky feel like a place you could *understand*, not only admire. I no longer remember the edition. I remember the voice: patient, concrete, unwilling to replace a hard idea with a metaphor and walk away. It treated the universe as something that could be explained to a curious person without insulting them, and without pretending that explanation is the same as poetry. After that, classroom physics stopped feeling like a closed club. Vectors were a way to talk about motion without waving your hands. Spectra were a way to ask a star what it was made of. Orbits stopped looking like decoration. I still write for that reader: someone who looked up, got hooked, and wanted the next sentence to be true. Public science is the same subject, spoken in a register that does not require a degree to enter the room. If you want a place to start among my notes, begin with [RIP Pluto](/writing/rip-pluto).

--- title: Wonders of the Outer System description: My tour of the cold worlds beyond the asteroid belt — Saturn’s rings, ice giants, and the crowded dark of the Kuiper Belt. date: 2026-04-01 published: true --- Most popular accounts of the solar system linger near the Sun: Mercury’s scorched rock, Earth’s blue luck, Mars as the nearest unfinished story. I wrote *Wonders of the Outer System* to start where the warmth thins out — past the asteroid belt, into gas giants, ice, and distances measured in light-hours. The book is my guided walk through Jupiter’s violence, Saturn’s geometry, Uranus and Neptune’s sideways weather, and the swarm of small worlds that refuse to behave like a neat ninth planet. Saturn sits at the emotional center for me: a planet whose rings make orbital mechanics visible to anyone willing to look carefully. Each chapter pairs a place with a rule. Why rings stay thin. Why moons shepherd ice. Why a dwarf planet can be geologically alive and still fail a classroom definition. I wanted a coherent picture of a neighborhood that is mostly empty space and a few spectacular exceptions, not a catalog of trivia. If you have only ever met the outer solar system as a list of names after Mars, this is the book I wrote to turn that list into a map. It is colder and sparser than the posters suggested.

---
title: Why Anything Happens
description: My book on forces, chance, and the small set of rules that turn empty space into stars, planets, and a night sky worth explaining.
date: 2025-09-20
published: true
---

Physics can sound like a museum of special cases: gravity here, electromagnetism there, quantum rules in a locked room at the back. I wrote *Why Anything Happens* to put the cases back into one story — how a handful of interactions, plus time, produce a universe that looks complicated from the inside.

I begin with motion and force in plain language, then widen to fields, probability, and the uncomfortable fact that “empty” is still governed. Not every reader wants the full mathematical machinery. The machinery still has a shape you can feel without a blackboard.

When the machinery does show up, it can stay small. Newton’s second law is just:

$$
F = ma
$$

And a few familiar scales help keep the story honest:

| Quantity | Rough scale | Why it matters |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Earth–Sun light time | ~8 minutes | “Near” in solar-system talk |
| Earth surface $g$ | $9.8\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$ | Everyday falling |
| Solar escape (Earth orbit) | ~42 km/s | Leaving the neighborhood |

The chapters move from falling apples to orbiting moons to the statistical quiet of atoms that refuse classical certainty. The through-line is cause: what makes one outcome more likely than another, and why the sky we inherit is the residue of lawful processes.

Read it as a companion to the outer-system book if you want the *where*; read it alone if you want the *why*.

New Next.js project only (same flow as https://ui.shadcn.com/create):
  npx shadcn@latest init --template next -y "https://uiception.com/r/portfolio-v1.json"

This scaffolds Next.js + shadcn, then installs the full site (app routes, content, components).

Then set BASIN_ENDPOINT in .env.local. Edit your name/bio/social links in app/page.tsx and app/layout.tsx. Writing posts live in content/writing/*.mdx and books live in content/books/*.mdx. MDX supports GFM tables and LaTeX math ($inline$ / $$block$$) via remark-gfm, remark-math, and rehype-katex.
